name: The Halo Effect
statement: One good impression bleeds into judgements of unrelated qualities.
statementAccent: bleeds into judgements of unrelated qualities
meaning: When we form a general impression of a person, brand, or product, that impression colours how we rate their specific, unrelated traits. Think someone is generally good and we assume their intelligence, honesty, and competence are good too, even without evidence for any of them.
mechanism: It is a cognitive bias in which one salient trait, or a global gut feeling, colours all the separate judgements that should be independent, so evaluations of distinct qualities become correlated when they ought not to be. The evaluator fails, in Thorndike's framing, to treat a person as a compound of independent qualities. The influence usually runs unconsciously: people do not realise their overall impression is driving their specific ratings.

examples.text: Dion, Berscheid and Walster (1972) found people rated physically attractive individuals as having more desirable personalities and likely to lead better, more successful lives: the foundational demonstration of the physical-attractiveness halo.

Nisbett and Wilson (1977) had students watch an instructor behave warmly or coldly, then rate his appearance, mannerisms, and accent. Those who saw the warm version found these unrelated attributes appealing; those who saw the cold version found the very same traits irritating, and were unaware of the influence.

A positive impression of one product lifts perception of a company's others, the 'iPod halo' often cited for Apple, and a celebrity's image transfers to whatever they endorse. These are standard applied illustrations rather than single controlled experiments.

variants.name: The horn effect
variants.text: The negative mirror image: a single disliked trait drags down perception of all the others, so one flaw taints the whole.

variants.name: The physical-attractiveness stereotype
variants.text: The well-studied subtype in which good looks confer assumed sociability, competence, intelligence, and trustworthiness: the 'beautiful is good' line of research.

variants.name: The halo effect in business analysis
variants.text: Phil Rosenzweig's argument (2007) that observers read a company's specific attributes (strategy, culture, leadership) off its overall performance, so success stories credit traits that are really just inferred from the outcome.

whyItMatters: It is one of the most robust and consequential biases in judgement, distorting hiring, grading, courtroom verdicts, marketing, and management analysis alike. Naming it is the first defence: knowing that a single strong impression can quietly colour every other rating is what lets evaluators try to score qualities on their own merits.

working.text: assess distinct attributes separately, ideally with structured criteria and by different people, so one strong impression cannot colour the rest.
when someone scores uniformly high or low across unrelated traits, suspect a halo (or horn) rather than genuine all-round excellence or failure.
when analysing a successful firm or person, ask whether the admired traits were measured independently or simply read back from the result.

limits: The core bias is real, robust, and replicated across roughly a century of research, but the term is often invoked loosely in popular and business writing to explain almost any favourable association without evidence. Its direction and strength are context-dependent: attractiveness-halo effect sizes vary by domain and outcome, and Nisbett and Wilson's effect was strong for some attributes and weaker for others. Rosenzweig's critique is itself a caution: much 'halo' talk in management reflects outcome-driven reasoning rather than a cleanly measured bias.
misreadings: It is not merely that we like attractive or successful people. It is that a global impression covertly alters judgements of logically separate traits, usually without the evaluator's awareness. Nor is it licence to label every positive association a 'halo'; the well-established core is a measured bias, not a catch-all for any favourable impression.
origin: Named and first measured by Edward L. Thorndike in his 1920 paper 'A Constant Error in Psychological Ratings' (Journal of Applied Psychology), in which officers rating soldiers on separate qualities produced correlations too high and even to be independent. Thorndike wrote that ratings were affected by a tendency to think of the person as generally good or inferior and to colour the specific judgements by that overall feeling.

sources.text: Thorndike, E.L. (1920). "A Constant Error in Psychological Ratings." Journal of Applied Psychology, 4, 25–29.
